name: Blackpipe Corridor
description:
Sarnia was already called Chemical Valley before the world ended and reassembled itself into corporate fiefdoms. The petrochemical plants that lined the St. Clair River in the twentieth century have been replaced by something worse: bioprocessing facilities, neural-substrate refineries, and atmospheric reclamation plants that claim to clean the air while producing the chemicals that dirty it. Ouroboros Energy and Cinderfall Energy maintain competing sovereign enclaves here, their territories marked by different-colored warning lights on the stacks — red for Ouroboros, amber for Cinderfall. The rivalry is not a metaphor. Workers have died in jurisdictional gaps between the two.

The Blackpipe Corridor stretches roughly 30 kilometers along the river, a continuous industrial strip where the distinction between 'factory' and 'city' dissolved decades ago. Residential blocks are built in the shadows of processing towers, and the rent is cheap because the air isn't. Atmospheric filtration masks are standard equipment — not augmentation, not fashion, just the baseline cost of breathing here. The population is predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2 workers bound by employment contracts that would be illegal in any jurisdiction that still enforced labor law. Cancer rates are three times the GLMZ average. The corponations attribute this to 'legacy contamination' from the pre-corporate era, which is technically true and practically a lie.

The river itself is the border. On the other side, Port Huron and the American shore. Between them, automated cargo barges move chemical precursors, refined neural substrates, and sealed containers that nobody asks about. The St. Clair River has been widened, deepened, and reinforced with automated navigation systems — it is less a river now than a liquid highway, and the things it carries are worth more per liter than the water itself. The Aamjiwnaang First Nation territory persists as a sovereign enclave within the Corridor, a legal anomaly that predates corporate sovereignty and that nobody has been able to dissolve despite decades of trying. They monitor the contamination with equipment the corponations don't control, and they publish the results.

sights: Processing tower stacks belching filtered exhaust — white plumes that look clean and aren't
Red and amber warning lights marking the Ouroboros-Cinderfall border, visible for kilometers
The St. Clair River choked with automated cargo barges, hull-to-hull in peak hours
Workers in atmospheric filtration masks walking between residential blocks and plant gates
The Aamjiwnaang monitoring station, bristling with independent sensors, a middle finger made of data
sounds: The constant industrial hum — a chord of machinery that changes pitch but never stops
Pressure release valves cycling on the processing towers — sudden hisses that become background
Barge navigation pings on the river, an automated conversation between machines
Atmospheric quality alerts broadcast on public speakers — the voice is calm, the numbers are not
smells: Petrochemical baseline — sweet, synthetic, and wrong in a way your body recognizes before your mind does
Neural substrate processing byproducts — metallic and sharp, like licking a battery
The river on hot days, carrying its own chemical biography upstream
atmosphere.feel: A place where the air itself is a negotiation between industry and survival. Everyone here knows the contamination numbers. Everyone here stays anyway, because the contracts pay and the alternatives don't. The Corridor doesn't pretend to be anything other than what it is — a machine for converting human labor and natural resources into corporate profit, with the waste products externalized into the bodies of the people who live here.

demographics: Population 280,000, predominantly Tier 1 contract workers and their families. The Aamjiwnaang enclave holds roughly 4,000 people — the most legally protected and least economically powerful residents. Average worker tenure is 7 years before health complications force contract termination. Replacement is constant.
economy: Petrochemical processing, neural-substrate refinement, and atmospheric reclamation. Ouroboros Energy and Cinderfall Energy account for 85% of employment. The remaining 15% is support economy — medical clinics, equipment repair, and the bars where contract workers spend their hazard pay.
power_structure: Dual-corporate sovereignty with a vestigial Canadian municipal overlay. Ouroboros and Cinderfall maintain separate security forces, separate medical systems, and separate environmental reporting. The Aamjiwnaang enclave operates under pre-corporate treaty rights that neither corporation can legally override — which doesn't stop them from trying.
dangers: Atmospheric contamination events — the filters fail, the alerts come late, the clinic queues grow
Jurisdictional gaps between Ouroboros and Cinderfall territories where no security responds
Contract enforcement — break your employment agreement and your housing, medical coverage, and legal status evaporate simultaneously
River accidents involving chemical cargo barges — the spill protocols protect the cargo first and the people second
Long-term neural substrate exposure — the refineries produce augmentation components, and the workers absorb the byproducts
opportunities: Environmental data from the Aamjiwnaang monitors is worth a fortune to the right buyers — lawyers, journalists, competing corps
Smuggling chemical precursors across the river to Port Huron
Contract mediation — workers trapped in exploitative agreements will pay to get out
story_hooks: The Aamjiwnaang monitoring data shows contamination levels that would trigger mandatory evacuation — if anyone with authority acknowledged the numbers
A Cinderfall processing tower has been producing an unregistered compound at night, and the barges carrying it cross the river with falsified manifests
Workers in the neural substrate refineries are developing synchronized augmentation glitches — not malfunction, but emergent behavior

adjacent_to: New Windsor / Novaya Windsorka (west along the corridor)
Port Huron (across the St. Clair River)
The Trans-Canada Corridor (east toward London and Toronto)

Chemical smugglers working the river crossings
Corporate security from both Ouroboros and Cinderfall
